content: Cranberries contain compounds known as proanthocyanidins (PACs), which have the ability to prevent p-fimbriated Escherichia coli from adhering to the urothelial cells that line the bladder. This mechanism has led to the widespread use of cranberry products over the past several decades as a preventive measure against urinary tract infections (UTIs). This review represents the fifth update of a systematic analysis originally published in 1998, with subsequent updates in 2003, 2004, 2008, and 2012. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of cranberry products in preventing UTIs among populations at risk. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in the Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Specialised Register up to March 13, 2023. The search included databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, as well as clinical trial registries and conference proceedings. The review included all randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs that compared cranberry products to placebo, no treatment, or other interventions such as antibiotics or probiotics. Data from the included studies were independently assessed and extracted by at least two authors. Information was collected on study methods, participant characteristics, interventions, and outcomes, including the incidence of symptomatic UTIs, positive urine cultures, side effects, and adherence to therapy. Risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated, and study quality was assessed using the Cochrane risk of bias tool. The certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. This update added 26 new studies, bringing the total to 50 studies involving 8,857 randomized participants. The risk of bias was generally low for sequence generation, allocation concealment, performance bias, and detection bias in many studies. Of the 50 studies, 45 compared cranberry products to placebo, water, or no specific treatment across six different participant groups. Twenty-six of these studies were included in a meta-analysis focusing on the outcome of symptomatic, culture-verified UTIs. The evidence suggests that cranberry products reduce the risk of UTIs in certain populations. Specifically: In women with recurrent UTIs, cranberry products probably reduce the risk of symptomatic, culture-verified UTIs (8 studies, 1,555 participants: RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.99; moderate certainty evidence). In children, cranberry products likely reduce the risk of UTIs (5 studies, 504 participants: RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.68; moderate certainty evidence). In individuals with susceptibility to UTIs due to medical interventions, cranberry products likely reduce the risk of UTIs (6 studies, 1,434 participants: RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.61; moderate certainty evidence). However, cranberry products appear to provide little or no benefit in other populations: In elderly institutionalized men and women, there was no significant reduction in the risk of UTIs (3 studies, 1,489 participants: RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.30; moderate certainty evidence). In pregnant women, cranberry products did not significantly reduce the risk of UTIs (3 studies, 765 participants: RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.50; moderate certainty evidence). In adults with neuromuscular bladder dysfunction and incomplete bladder emptying, there was no significant reduction in the risk of UTIs (3 studies, 464 participants: RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.19; low certainty evidence). When compared to antibiotics, cranberry products may have little or no effect on the risk of symptomatic, culture-verified UTIs (2 studies, 385 participants: RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.33; low certainty evidence). Similarly, there was no significant difference in the risk of clinical symptoms without culture confirmation (2 studies, 336 participants: RR 1.30, 95% CI 0.79 to 2.14; low certainty evidence). However, when compared to probiotics, cranberry products may reduce the risk of symptomatic, culture-verified UTIs (3 studies, 215 participants: RR 0.39, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.56; moderate certainty evidence). The review also examined the form and dosage of cranberry products. It remains unclear whether cranberry juice is more or less effective than cranberry tablets, or whether different doses of PACs have varying efficacy, as the certainty of the evidence in these comparisons was very low. Gastrointestinal side effects were reported, but the number of participants experiencing these side effects was likely similar between those taking cranberry products and those receiving placebo or no treatment (10 studies, 2,166 participants: RR 1.33, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.77; moderate certainty evidence). Additionally, there was no clear relationship between adherence to cranberry therapy and the risk of recurrent UTIs. In conclusion, the updated evidence supports the use of cranberry products to reduce the risk of symptomatic, culture-verified UTIs in women with recurrent UTIs, children, and individuals at risk due to medical interventions. However, cranberry products do not appear to be effective in elderly individuals, pregnant women, or those with bladder emptying problems.
